projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Edward D'Alessandro was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Edward A. D'Alessandro. Mr. D'Alessandro served in the U.S. Army with the 10th Army, 24th Corps. He served stateside and in Korea, and his highest rank was corporal. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. D'Alessandro's home in Westlake, Ohio, on September 16th, 2003. Ed was 90 at the time of this recording. Ed passed away in February of 2004.

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: In 1941, I was living at 10713 Elmira Avenue, which ran parallel to Loraine Avenue; and the closest landmark would have been the old Sears and Roebuck store that was at 110th and Loraine. That is the streetcar that I took going to work and coming back, and then walking down 110th to Elmira, where my home was. We lived in a, what was then known as a bungalow, one-story bungalow, with full basement. It was six rooms. I was not married. I was living with my parents at the time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's see. You would have been in your twenties. You were working, I assume?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: I was working at the Cleveland Public Library. And in 1941, on Pearl Harbor Day, December 7th, I had spent the evening, the night with my older brother, Dr. Nicholas S. D'Alessandro, who lived at, out on a street called Dorothy Avenue, off of Rocky River Drive. I had babysat his daughter while he and his wife had gone out; and having risen early that morning, we were having breakfast when we heard the announcement that the Japanese had bombed Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction when you heard that news?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: My reaction at that time was that we were finally at war, and that it would not be very long before my brother and I, Dr. Arthur, who was just finishing his residency in surgery at Charity Hospital, would be involved. At that time, I would be -- '41, let's see, I was born in 1913. How old would that have made me?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: I would have been 28 years old, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you tempted to go out the next day and sign up?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: At that particular time, no. Because I was the only one living at home, and the only one who was taking care of my parents. The others were married and were busy raising their own families. And I felt responsible for my parents. And at the time, I was the youngest branch librarian in the Cleveland Public Library. I was in charge of the Woodland branch, as head librarian, at 5806 Woodland Avenue. And at the time, I believe teachers and librarians, as educators, were considered necessary to be kept on the home front. But that changed before very long.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. So how long was it before you were drafted?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: First of all, could you have gotten a deferrment as supporting -- because there were other kids?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: No, no, no, no. I never considered the deferrment. I, I let the normal process take its course, just like it did. My draft number came up in the early spring of 1943. And I was drafted into the military service, actually on the 13th of May, 1943.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember doing anything for the war effort before you were drafted?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Yes. Yes. In the library, before I became branch librarian, in the early days of the war, I was at the time a reference and research librarian in the sociology division of the main librarian, library. And at that time, this was 1941, no, 19 -- before 1931 (sic), it was some time in 1940. At the time, the assistant director of the Cleveland Library was a man by the name of Russell Munn; and he came to me one day and, at that time, and said, "We have to do something to promote the war effort," or "to help in the war effort here in the main library." And he felt that we ought to establish a reading center on the second floor in the main lobby between the two elevators, that would help with information on the war effort. And he decided the center should be named War and Defense Information Center. And I was put in charge of getting the materials together and setting that, that up. And very often I was scheduled to serve people who had need of information that was there at the time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This was in 1940, then?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: This was in the early days before we got into the war.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So this would be a collection of newspapers, magazines, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Magazines, books. We had to bring together books that were apropos from the various divisions in the main library. We had the library shop build shelves in that little alcove between the, that existed between the elevators. It's still there. I mean the alcove is still there, not the center. And we filled that with books and magazines and pamphlets and other information that would have some use in, and help in the war effort.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there a lot of public interest in the war, before we got into it?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Oh yes. Oh yes. There was. There was great interest in the original position of our country with regard to the war. I can recall definitely the days when Churchill was trying to get the United States into it, and Franklin Roosevelt was keeping us out of the war, saying that he would, he would help the British effort by lend lease. That was a great thing then, lend lease, when he, I think he arranged to have some 23 ships shipped over to Great Britain to help in the war effort. And he did what he could through financial aid and supplies and what have you, and the war effort. And of course, we were pushed into the war when Pearl, when Pearl Harbor occurred, Japanese pulled that dastardly attack on Pearl Harbor. And we lost so many, so many men, and a greater part of our fleet was destroyed. And one of my good friends, Ensign Haloran, who was aboard the battleship Arizona, went down with that ship. He, that's when it came close to home, as far as I was concerned, having a friend die.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long was it before you found out that he actually did perish on that ship?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Oh, almost immediately.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You did find out?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Oh yeah, yeah. We lived close by. He lived in the general area that I lived in. He lived down along the 117th area, off of --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember rationing being much of a problem before you went into the service?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: No. Not before I went into the service. I have no, no experience with rationing, 'cause I was away during most of it. Because rationing had begun before I went in, but it had not reached its, what will I say, height, until after I had gone into the service.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So any involvement in scrap drives, or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: We, we did what we could to save materials. All kinds of materials that we could save. And the kind of effort we did, promoted the saving of things through, through projects and programs in the library. At the time, as I was a young professional, as I indicated, in the library, and my younger brother, Dr. Arthur, was just finishing his, his second or third year of residency at Charity Hospital; and I can recall that I received my call-in in the spring and went in in May, and he got his call and went in in July of '43. He went the other way. Eventually, after serving one, one, a little over about a year or so in this country, as a, personally as a Army librarian at Drew Field, Florida, after having basic training at Gulfport Field in Mississippi, I was shipped to Drew Field, Florida, where I was a, an Army librarian, and worked in the Army library there for about a year. And then when we were having great need for replacements in the infantry, a group of us that were in special services were transferred into the infantry. The Air Corps at the time was part of the U.S. Army, was not a separate unit as it is now, or special arm of the service as it is now. It was known as the U.S. Army Air Corps. And so there were about 33 of us who were considered 1-A, physically fit, were transferred out of the Air Corps at Drew Field, and we were shipped to Camp Gordon, Georgia, for infantry training. I went through -- even though I had had nine weeks or so of infantry training in the Air Corps, I went through another nine weeks at that Camp Gordon, Georgia, and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any unusual or interesting stories during your training, either in basic training or later infantry training?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Oh yes, yes. When we were at Camp Gordon, Georgia, we were being readied, the rumors began very early that we were going to be readied for the invasion of Japan. And it persisted through my entire stay in Camp Gordon. And it finally came to a, a head when we were assigned to a heavy weapons company. The heavy weapons consisted of the 81-millimeter mortar. That's that big tube, where we fired 25-pound shells in the tube, tube and a tripod and a base plate, you know. And we were shipped off from Camp Gordon, Georgia. Then it became a fact that we were being readied to be the first troops to invade Japan. We were shipped to Camp Maxey, Texas, for invasion training. And from there, we were shipped to Fort Ord, California, and we were assigned to the 24th Corps of the 10th Army as replacements. Which was to be one of two armies that were to spearhead into Japan. The 10th Army was supposed to spear, go in, we understood, from Okinawa, into Japan, and the 8th Army was supposed to come from Guam. And we were ready, ready for shipment on the troop ships when Truman dropped the bomb. And instead of going in as invasion troops, our, our convoys of troop ships went in as occupation troops. We first came into the, into Yokohama Bay, and a great number of troops were left off there. This was right after the signing of the surrender with the Japanese. MacArthur had signed the surrender on September 2nd, 1945. And by the part of, latter part of September, early October, we were landing in Inchon. Those of us that were kept aboard the troop ships after they left the troops off in Japan, we went around the islands into South Korea, and we were the first troops to occupy South Korea. And we were in Inchon, which was just, just blow the, on the coast, just blow the 38th Parallel, not too far from Seoul, Korea, and went -- when we arrived there, they did some more reassignments, and -- oh, when we arrived in the, in the waters just off of the coast of South Korea, we were told there was no way that we might not have a problem in landing; that we didn't know whether we were going to face some kind of opposition or not; 'cause there were still quite a number of Japanese soldiers in South Korea, you see. Japan had been, well, Japan had had Korea under its foot for 35 years. And so South Korea was, was virtually a subjugated country under, under Japan for all those years. And so we had no, we were told there was no way that we, we would know whether we were going to have some opposition or not. So when we -- we were not able to, because of the tide, not able to go right into port. We stopped just some distance out at sea, and in full regalia, rifles, helmet, and 60-pound backpack, we had to climb down by the cargo nets down the side of the ship, and then jump into the landing barge, what did they call those, the Higgins?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Higgins boat?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Higgins boats. And of course we had to watch that we didn't get, fall in between, you know. We've had to jump at the right time off of the cargo net into the Higgins boat. And then we landed in Korea in that way. We found no opposition. And as we, as we marched into the city of Inchon, the South Koreans came rushing up to us saying, "Me no Korea -- me no Japanese," or "me no Japanese, me Korean, me Korean." They wanted to be sure we knew they weren't Japanese. And so of course the first, first job was the evacuation and the sending back all the Japanese that were there, back to Japan. And for the first several months that we were there doing that, we, we were billetted in squad tents; and then, when we got the Japanese out and evacuated quarters that they were occupying, we finally had some decent quarters to move in, move our cots in, and had some decent billets.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did any of them give you any trouble, the Japanese soldiers?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: No. No trouble at all. Absolutely no trouble. And, but you know, it was very interesting, though. We weren't there very long when, when the, even though they, we weren't causing any trouble, we had very good relations with the locals. In fact, we were feeding them. They had been virtually -- I saw children there with this, the extended bellies and legs, you know, like the rungs of a chair, you know. Because they weren't, you know, treated very well by the Japanese. And we, we did, typically American, we treated them well, and so. But even with that, after a couple of months, some of the Korean natives would say to us, "When are you going home?" And I can recall feeling, well, who in the world in their right minds in any country would want foreign troops on their soil, you know? We weren't causing any trouble. We were, we were a benevolent occupying force. There was no problem there, like we read about now in Iraq. And it was interesting to note that the Russians had beat us in over the 38th parallel. They were there when we arrived. And so you know, when we pulled guard duty along the line of demarcation there, we, we could virtually yell across and speak to the Russian troops, you know, that were doing their guard duty on the other side. But they didn't waste any time. They were there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Never had any trouble with the Russians?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: No. We never had any trouble. There's only one, one time when there might have been, not with the Russians, when we, when there was some kind of a rumor on the first New Years Eve that we were there, that there might be trouble with some members of the populace. And we were issued our live ammunition again, and to be ready for any trouble. No trouble occurred. It was a peaceful occupation. We had no trouble. We found Korea in very bad shape, South Korea. The sanitation was, well, virtually nil. And of course they still, still had the honey carts, I can remember, that went around collecting the human excrement from buildings, with these big long shovels, and put them in these big barrels on ox-drawn carts; and then they would take them out into the, into the fields, where they used it as fertilizer. And I can recall having come so accustomed to that smell that, even when I got home, after awhile, for awhile I still thought I had that smell in my nostrils, you know. But at any rate, my stay there wasn't, wasn't too long; because Truman finally developed the point system for discharge. You see, in World War II, we were in for the duration. We weren't in for a year or two years or 18 months or what have you. We were in for the duration, however long they needed us, you know. And so we would be saying to one another, while we were in Korea, even after we were there six months, "When are we going home? We going to be stuck here forever?" You know. Because it was not a very, very appetizing place to be in at the time, from the standpoint of, as I said, sanitation. And I can recall one day walking, walking through the area there, around, we called the area that we were in our, that we were billetted in Ascom City. We Americans have a way of giving names to places where they live, even though they're overseas. And I was walking down the road in Ascom City, and a G.I. vehicle went by, and dust rose up, and I got something in my eye. The next morning, I woke up, my right eye was shut tight. I had had an infection in my eye that took several weeks for the Army medics to clear up. That was because they, people did number one, number two right in the roadways, you know. And it was not a very sanitary situation, for a long time. But, being occupied by the Americans, South Korea became a very vital, economic, strongly economic community, or country of its own; while on the other hand, North Korea, that had been occupied by the Russians and had become communist, became the problem situation that it is now. That, in my mind, as a person who was a thinking person, often felt that our powers that be that separated Germany into two, East and West Germany, and Korea into South and North Germany (sic), made such an awful big mistake.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Backtracking a bit --

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your reaction when you heard that they had dropped the atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: My reaction was, well, at the time, we all knew we were going to be the first troops to go in; and my reaction was, god bless Truman, because he saved our lives. Frankly, between you and me here as we sit, I wouldn't be here today talking to you if Truman hadn't dropped that bomb. Because we were going to be the, as they had projected then, part of that 500,000 of us that they were ready to lose in the invasion of Japan. And we were going to be the first wave to go in. And of course you all know what happened to the first wave that, first waves that went into Normandy. I would be over there somewhere pushing up daisies, not here talking to you today. So to me, no one can say anything bad about Mr. Truman. He saved not only a lot of American lives, my life and others like me, but a lot of Japanese lives; because, had he not dropped the bomb, the war would have gone on longer. It would have continued, because there would have been more loss of life on both sides. So anybody who I designate as bleeding hearts start saying the United States was bad in dropping the bomb, huh-uh. The good of it far outweighs the bad in it. The war would have gone on a long time longer. So here I am. I wouldn't be here talking to you today.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, do you remember where you were when F.D.R. died and your reaction to that news?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Yes. That was April of 1945. We were, at that time I was at Camp Gordon, Georgia, in training. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And that's not -- is that close to Warm Springs or not?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wasn't he at Warm Springs, Georgia at one time?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: He was in Warm Springs, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was the reaction from the guys sadness, or was it, you know, heard about too many friends being lost during the war --

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: No, I think there was, the people, the soldiers I was with, we had all been people who had voted for Franklin Roosevelt and believed in Franklin Roosevelt, what he had been doing. So there was, there was sadness on our part. I don't want to, I don't recall hearing very much of anybody not feeling sad about his passing, where I was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about your time during the, when you were in the service, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Let's see. I was in the service for about three years, wasn't I? 'Cause I came home -- I left in the spring of '43 and came home in the spring of '46. I think probably one of the happiest times in my life was the, was the fact that, when Truman announced -- I can, I'll never forget his words. A message came through to us from headquarters when we were in Korea, and, indicating Truman, President Truman has felt so strongly that he wants to bring home his citizens army as soon as possible. Citizens army. Those words still stick with me. Has, for that reason, developed the point system. And at the time, I didn't know how many points I had yet; because headquarters was going to be figuring that out, you see. And this was, oh, when was this? Some time in early '46, when the announcement came. And then, lo and behold, the day of great happiness for me was when I was informed that I had enough points to go home. And I was told to report to the port of Inchon, to the mustering out area, for initial processing. And I can recall spending three or four days there before they put us on a troop ship to come back home; and I can recall boarding the U.S.S. Admiral Eberle, E-b-e-r-l-e, troop ship, and coming home on that troop ship. By the way, I've written a book that includes some of that stuff. Of course, I've written two books. I'm now working on my third book.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I didn't realize that.

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You selling copies?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Well, there, you can see the one, it's called "My Father Was a Tailor." Actually, it's autobiographical. It's on the top shelf, if you can go over and pick it up. And it tells much of this story, but in kind of capsule form. "My Father Was a Tailor," yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. That's very nice.

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Yeah. That was published in 1999.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: My first book was published in 1988. And I'm working on one now, growing up in -- I don't know whether you know that there was a place once upon a time in downtown Cleveland called Big Italy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, I didn't know.

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: In the old hay market. Did you know there was an old hay market there? Well, that's all in here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Before my time I guess, huh?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Well, Big Italy, I'm writing, this book that I'm writing now is called "Once Upon a Time in Big Italy."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That sounds good.

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Yeah, this tells -- oh, this also includes pictures, when my brother and I were in the Army; and it shows my brother, Art, doing surgery on a wounded soldier in Normandy. 'Cause he went in, into Europe, and he was a battlefield surgeon.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any big celebrations on V.J. day, when the war finally ended?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: No, I wasn't involved in any of that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was pretty quiet where you were?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's a pretty good photo. Was that taken by the Signal Corps?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Which was?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The picture of your brother?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: The picture of my brother doing surgery on a wounded soldier, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Courtesy of Press Association, so it was taken by --

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, that appeared in Collier's Magazine.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh wow.

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: During the Normandy, during the height of Normandy, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. This is a good-looking book.

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Yeah, there's a picture there when I was at Camp Gordon in infantry training, following the pictures that -- no, no, that's right, right following the --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where I was?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Where you were. No, up further.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Up further?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wedding day.

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: No, it's earlier. I got married after we --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Army of occupation.

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: That's when I was in, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: There's Camp Gordon?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Camp Gordon. That's, that's when we were invasion training in Camp --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your outfit again?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your outfit?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: I was in the 24th Corps of the 10th Army.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your specific job after you were a librarian? When you were overseas, what was your job? Did you have a specific job, or --

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: I was an infantryman, until we arrived in Korea. Then we were transferred, I was transferred into the Quartermaster Corps. 545th Quartermaster Corps, I was what they called ration breakdown non-com. I was in charge of issuing food to the troops. All the mess sergeants came to me when I was in Korea for, with their tally-out sheets for food. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Very good. You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: That covers it. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Covered a lot of it there, too, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Excellent.

sp.speaker: Edward D'Alessandro
sp.p: Yeah.
